prompt: Classify each code snippet or scenario by the security issue it represents — or mark it as safe.

items.explanation: User input is interpolated directly into the query string, so an attacker can send something like "1 OR 1=1" and change what the query actually does. Parameterized queries fix this.
Untrusted input is injected straight into the HTML response with no escaping, so an attacker can submit a <script> tag that runs in another user's browser.

items.task: Storing the user's password as-is in the database after registration
items.explanation: Passwords must be hashed (with bcrypt) before storage. If the database is ever breached, plain-text passwords hand an attacker every account immediately — and probably other accounts too, since people reuse passwords.
This is a parameterized query — the database receives the SQL and the value separately, so user input can never become part of the query structure.
This compares a plain-text password directly, which means storedPassword isn't hashed, and the === comparison isn't constant-time — both are real problems. Use bcrypt.compare() instead.
textContent sets text, not HTML, so a string like "<script>" is rendered as literal visible text instead of being parsed and executed. This is the standard fix for the XSS pattern above.
Secrets belong in environment variables, not committed source code. A hardcoded key is exposed to anyone with repository access, and stays exposed in git history even after it's removed.

items.task: const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 10); // stored in DB
items.explanation: This is exactly the right pattern: hash the password with bcrypt before storing it, so the original password is never saved anywhere.
